title: Proton's ScopeIdAllocation::run verification is too limiting
body:
### Describe the bug

At https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/bad25767a03107bc23e066d94aca489dc86ca70c/third_party/proton/Dialect/lib/Analysis/ScopeIdAllocation.cpp#L36 the verifier in the compiler checks that for every exit scope it encounters, a valid enter scope has already been seen. This prevents code that is dynamically correct but lexically "misordered", such as this:


```python
initialized = False

for i in range(0, 2):
	if initialized:
		wait_init_completion()
		pl.exit_scope("whatever")

	pl.enter_scope("whatever")
	do_init()
	initialized = True
```

While this is a contrived example, our pipeline construction does generate cases like these and makes it difficult to profile traces like these using Proton.

### Environment details

Triton: main
GPU: GH200

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:

We are aware of the problem and thus do not recommend instrumenting loops if the triton semantic is enabled. In this case, it would be better to instrument ttgir

> This is an explicit software pipeline; we're using Gluon and this is what our pipelining tools emit in some cases

I don't get it. If using gluon then isn't pipelining generated by the user? If you are building your own pipelining tool on top of it, I guess it has to be proton aware.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Yes, the pipeline is something that we generate. Here's an example of why you might have something like this (pseudocode):

```python3
for some_range:
	# pre-load stage (actually sets things up for compute)
	copy.wait()
	pl.exit_scope("load")
	pl.enter_scope("compute")
	scaled = smem.load() * 2

	# load stage
	pl.enter_scope("load")
	copy = async_copy(smem)

	# compute stage
	dot(scaled, whatever)
	pl.exit_scope("compute")
```

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Yeah, unfortunately in this case the pipeliner has to be aware of profiling.

That is, you probably want to have the pipeliner generate exit_scope and enter_scope statements automatically like "load [stage=1]"

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
I'm not sure I understand. My problem is that execution does not always move forward because loops allow for backward branches. The walk that Proton does doesn't account for this and thinks an operation that completes "before" its start in the source code is illegal, even though this is possible inside of loops when the completion happens on a future iteration. I'm not even sure how I would set things up in my profiler to avoid this. In cases where I do a load first and then the compute which relies on the load with nothing in between, things work out. But any interesting schedule will run into this issue. In fact I would think that most schedules will, because if you do any work to reset the buffer (e.g. to rotate it, or pull data out before a new operation starts storing) you will have a control flow where you wait for the previous operation to complete, do your buffer reset, then issue the next stage. This is inherently "in the wrong order". Do you see a way to fix this?

Taking a step back, I'm not even sure I understand why this restriction is in place. Glancing at the code it seems like scopes have a concept of a "parent", but looking at the emitted trace I don't see any sign of this information. Personally if I was implementing this I would just have enter_scope and exit_scope write to a ring buffer and then when the kernel finishes I can reconstruct the sequence of scopes from that (assuming a well-behaved stack of enter/exit calls, which I can guarantee will happen at runtime). Is this not possible to do, or am I missing something?
